title: Intel Core Series 3 (Wildcat Lake) CPU at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Intel detailed Wildcat Lake, its first high-volume low-priced chiplet CPU, which reuses Panther Lake's Panther Cove and Darkmont cores and Xe3 GPU but drops to two dies on cheap organic MCP packaging with UCIe instead of Foveros. Intel skipped a process generation from Intel 7 to 18A, recovers about 29% of compute dies through harvesting SKUs, and reports over 70 design wins.

insights.claim: MCP organic packaging is the only way for Intel to hit its affordability targets while using a chiplet design, with UCIe as the enabling technology that let Intel avoid Foveros for die-to-die interconnect.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: UCIe over organic substrate becomes the volume chiplet path for cost-sensitive silicon, expanding the addressable market for standard-interface chiplets well beyond premium parts.
insights.quote: MCP/organic packaging is the only way for Intel to hit their affordability targets while using a chiplet design.
insights.locator: Packaging was apparently a hard decision for Intel

insights.claim: Advanced packaging has a pitch of about 36 microns while organic UCIe is around 110 micron, and the lower density die-to-die connection keeps costs down while matching the smaller amounts of data this chip moves.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies the density-versus-cost trade in chiplet interconnect, the key variable in deciding which products justify advanced packaging capacity.
insights.quote: Advanced packaging has a pitch of about 36 microns, organic UCIe is around 110 micron.
insights.locator: Advanced packaging has a pitch of about 36 microns

insights.claim: Intel evaluated a monolithic die and forgoing chiplets entirely, but IP availability and the actual costs of chiplet fabbing and assembly favored the 2 die MCP format.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Chiplets won on IP reuse and total cost even at the budget tier, suggesting monolithic client dies are on the way out across price points.
insights.quote: Intel did look at doing a monolithic die as well and forgoing chiplets entirely, but with IP availability and the actual costs of chiplet fabbing and assembly favored the 2 die MCP format.
insights.locator: For Wildcat Lake, Intel went down to just 2 dies

insights.claim: Wildcat Lake's package is quite a bit smaller than Panther Lake's and much cheaper by being organic multi-chip instead of Foveros.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Package cost savings flow straight to gross margin in a segment where BoM discipline decides whether Intel keeps the socket.
insights.locator: Wildcat Lake’s package is also quite a bit smaller

themes.theme: Latest architecture in a budget part

insights.claim: Rather than the usual budget approach of a generation-minus-one or minus-two design, Intel delivered its latest architecture to the budget market, giving Wildcat Lake Thunderbolt 4, the Xe3 GPU architecture, and Wi-Fi 7.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Pushing current-generation IP into entry-level parts compresses the price umbrella Intel's competitors have used to win budget sockets.
insights.quote: Much of the time the way to a budget chip is to do a gen -1 (or -2) design. But for this generation, Intel wanted to deliver their latest architecture to the budget market.
insights.locator: Core Series 3 is derived from Core Ultra Series 3

insights.claim: Intel skipped a generation of process nodes with Wildcat Lake, moving from Raptor Lake-U on Intel 7 to 18A.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A high-volume budget product on 18A is a meaningful capacity commitment and a broad real-world test of Intel's newest node.
insights.quote: Intel’s last generation product in this line was Raptor Lake-U, an Intel 7 process product. So they have skipped a generation of process nodes here, going from 7 to 18A.
insights.locator: Core Series 3 is derived from Core Ultra Series 3

insights.claim: Wildcat Lake is a distinct silicon design from Panther Lake but largely not a distinct architecture, reusing the Panther Cove and Darkmont CPU cores and the Xe3 GPU architecture scaled down.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: IP reuse across price tiers lowers Intel's per-SKU engineering cost, a structural response to margin pressure in client CPUs.
insights.locator: Wildcat Lake is notable here in that

insights.claim: Intel cut Panther Lake down with fewer P cores, fewer NPU engines, a smaller GPU, dropped ray tracing, removed cache, and downsized the display controller by removing DisplayPort UHBR capabilities, but kept the XMX cores despite initially wanting to drop them.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Retaining matrix engines in a budget part signals Intel expects on-device AI features to be table stakes even at entry price points.
insights.quote: Intel dropped ray tracing here, but they did keep the XMX cores (though they wanted to drop it initially).
insights.locator: Here’s a look at how Intel cut-down Panther Lake

insights.claim: Intel kept Thunderbolt 4/USB4 with just two heads, cut PCIe lanes, removed camera PHYs entirely, and left the validation-heavy globals unchanged, saving about 15% in die area for the I/O chiplet versus Panther Lake.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Only 15% I/O die savings shows how validation cost, not silicon area, constrains derivative designs.
insights.quote: Altogether this saved Intel about 15% in die area for the I/O chiplet versus Panther Lake.
insights.locator: As for IO, Intel kept Thunderbolt 4/USB4 connectivity

insights.claim: Intel went with a narrower DRAM bus to cut system vendor cost while keeping dedicated power rails for the E-cores and GPU, which drive Panther and Wildcat Lake energy efficiency, and keeping high integration of features like Wi-Fi 7 to hold down vendor system costs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shows Intel optimizing total system BoM rather than chip BoM, the metric that actually decides OEM design wins in budget laptops.
insights.locator: Intel opted to go with a narrower DRAM bus

insights.claim: UCIe forced Intel to learn how to efficiently packetize die-to-die communications, because Foveros is not packetized while UCIe is.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Protocol differences, not just physical pitch, carry the real migration cost when moving to standard chiplet interfaces.
insights.quote: Foveros is not packetized, whereas UCIe is.
insights.locator: UCIe also meant that Intel had to learn

insights.claim: Intel had to buffer the display links between dies so they could enter a low power state and burst data once buffers were full, because display traffic runs across the dies almost constantly on cheap laptops that lack panel self refresh.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete example of how low-cost system components create silicon design constraints, and why battery-life targets drove the D2D design.
insights.quote: They have to run display traffic across the dies almost constantly, in part because cheap laptops often don’t have panel self refresh
insights.locator: Power was another big concern for Intel

insights.claim: Keeping the UCIe links limited to an 8 GT/sec rate kept the bit error rate low enough to avoid retry and forward error correction, trading more die space for more lanes in exchange for lower complexity, which Intel judged the bigger risk.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Complexity risk, not area, was the binding constraint for a first UCIe implementation, a useful lesson for judging other vendors' chiplet timelines.
insights.quote: It ate up more die space by requiring a larger number of lanes, but it kept the complexity down, which was the bigger risk.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, keeping the links limited to an 8 GT/sec rate

insights.claim: Intel put a second LDO on the board as a signal-integrity backup plan that ended up not being needed and could be removed later.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Contingency components that get designed out post-launch are a small but real source of BoM improvement over a product's life.
insights.locator: And, of course, there is always the matter of signal integrity

insights.claim: About 29% of Wildcat Lake compute dies were recoverable with Intel's current chip SKUs, though SKUs customers do not want are not helpful to recovery in practice.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Die harvest rates only convert to margin when the harvested SKUs are sellable, a nuance often missed in yield-based cost models.
insights.quote: about 29% of compute dies were recoverable with their current chip SKUs. The balancing act is that SKUs that customers do not want (or are not useful) is not helpful to recovery in practice.
insights.locator: And here is a look at die yield recovery

insights.claim: Intel is already at over 70 design wins for Wildcat Lake, and the chip is on its way to replacing Raptor Lake-U as the backbone of Intel's budget processor offering.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Design-win count is the leading indicator of budget-segment volume and of whether 18A capacity gets absorbed.
insights.quote: Intel is already at over 70 design wins for Wildcat Lake, and the chip is well on its way to replacing Raptor Lake-U as the backbone of Intel’s budget processor offering.
insights.locator: Overall, Intel’s Wildcat Lake team is very proud

insights.claim: While the bulk of Wildcat Lake chips go into consumer devices, Intel also deploys them in a decent edge device market, making the part one end of a spectrum that runs from edge to data center Diamond Rapids.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Edge deployment gives budget client silicon a second, higher-margin demand channel that outlives consumer refresh cycles.
insights.locator: As the first of Intel’s triad of presentations
